I am no longer a Murakami virgin. He has had his way with me, it was painless, and I am more than satisfied while being left wanting more. I had mistakenly thought it would be a challenging read. Instead it was smooth and moved along like a bullet train. Though the novel is set in 21st century Japan, somehow having read The Makioka Sisters just a couple weeks earlier, I felt oriented in the country. Also the story opens with an incident that happened during WWII so at first it almost felt like I was reading a sequel. I loved the David Mitchell-style way that the story jumped back and forth in time and slowly revealed the connections between the characters. I loved the ghost story atmosphere, the references to music and literature both Japanese and American, but most of all I loved the characters, even the insane artist dad. Kafka himself is one of the greatest characters I have come across in all my years of reading. Just to prove that he is an evolved human male, Murakami also created several awesome and believable female characters. He takes the motherless boy trope to new heights. And yes, it is a metaphysical, magical realism, philosophical novel at the same time. Since all I can do is gush, I will end here.

In my humble opinion~ FOR WHO Those who are almost done learning N3 (pre intermediate Japanese). AIM Reading practice. HOW I FOUND IT I learnt about this book in GenkiJACS school. We read one of the chapters in class, and I decided to buy the book and read the rest on my own. HOW TO STUDY Ideally with a teacher. But you can still manage to read the main reading exercises and benefit from them alone. TRANSLATION There's nothing except JAPANESE in this book. ______ ABOUT THE BOOK: This book contains 12 chapters, and each chapter has a page-long reading exercise, vocabulary list, and quite a few discussion questions. It's suitable for people who are almost done studying N3 Japanese and before they start N2 Japanese. However, the book doesn't contain any english at all. This is a good thing (good reading practice) and a bad thing (you might misunderstand the meaning) at the same time. So get ready to get some intense research for translation of words and sentences done. Because of that, and the fact there are a lot of discussion questions that require a lot of proper grammar/vocabulary usage, I think this book is better to be studied with a teacher (so you wouldn't end up guessing the meaning of sentences wrong). I personally read the book alone without a teacher.. but I couldn't really answer the questions, as my answers will probably require correction and I'd rather not end up memorizing wrong answers/meanings. I think you'll get better use of the book if you had someone explaining the sentences to you and correcting your answers.. having a conversation flowing will benefit you greatly while learning from this book. Also some questions require a CD which isn't attached with the book.. you have to get it separately (I don't own it). Overall, I enjoyed this book. And I do recommend it if you want to practice reading in Japanese.

Reality in a Can If you're new to Philip K. Dick, then I can't recommend UBIK as a place to get to know him. Start with one of his inventive SciFi operas (Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? or The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch), his psychological conundrums (Confessions of a Crap Artist or A SCANNER DARKLY), his cold-war farces (The Zap Gun or The Simulacrum), or any of his fun short story collections. If you're familiar with Dick, you'll find that UBIK displays all of his hallmarks. 1) A what-if concept that is too simple for any other author to invent: in this case a corp of anti-psi characters who are in high demand because their ultra-mundane presence blocks psychic interference. 2) Hapless male protagonists controlled by feminine mystique. 3) Thurber-style humor, such as talking coin-op household appliances. And 4) exploration of the borderline personality. In this case, the borderline personality takes over the book as each character fades to a figment of another's imagination and reality itself is revealed to be the product of a spray can. Comment

** spoiler alert ** Stayed up all night reading this last night. First impressions: Awesome. Heartbreaking. No-holds-barred. Brutally honest. Need to let it sink in before I say anything else. * * * * And now, a month later, I blather a lot about this book. This is not the next best tween sparkling love story. This is not a Happy Ever After story. This is a story about broken people surviving the very best they can in a broken world. On first read, Mockingjay was a big old disappointment. However, after giving it some time to sink in, I'm left feeling a tremendous respect for Collins' choices. While I may be disappointed, the ending worked and it was the right ending. Anything else would have sold the story short. Mockingjay is the story of a broken girl. On first read, the book felt rushed, and disconnected from the action of what was happening. As a reader, I didn't feel as connected to what was happening, but now that I've had some time to reflect, I think that style ultimately reflected how disconnected Katniss was from what was happening around her. As the readers, we're connected to Katniss, and when Katniss isn't connected, we aren't either. She has two moments of complete connection, and both of those moments forever change the landscape of the world. I'm not sure she would have been compelled to do either if she hadn't been so damaged. Yeah, Gale gets a frustratingly brief mention, Finnick's death is like a footnote, and characters slide out of Katniss' life with barely a glance, but you know, it works because of how completely messed up she is. She's a veteran of war forced to compartmentalize the most basic of things to keep sane. If she can't feel it's because when she does feel, she ends up sobbing in a closet. I feel like her acceptance of Peeta and children are not examples of hope and healing but instead resignation. I can't help but wonder if she doesn't step into the role of wife and mother with the same submission she fell into the role of Mockingjay; thrust there by the needs of others more assertive and dominant than she is. This is just one more lottery she volunteers for. The liberated-free-the-people-kick-their-asses-blow-things-up entertainment junkie in me wanted Katniss to throw off the yoke of her slavery, rise up to become the Superwoman, president, female James Bond, kick-ass-take-names Big Ass Hero RAWR, but if I'm really honest with myself, the lover of really awesome stories no-matter-what in me would have been really mad if that had happened. I many not like what happened to Katniss, but I respect it. The story isn't less because of it, it's just not That story. There are plenty of Those stories out there if I want to read one. From the very beginning we know Katniss was never a super-hero, she was a media figurehead monopolized into fulfilling the role of Civil War Music Video Poster Girl. No different really than a Brittney Spears' Buy my Album or Abercrombie and Fitch Buy this Shirt campaign. Katniss was the Buy this War Girl campaign model. Katniss wasn't selected to be the media darling because of how awesomely talented she was, she was selected because of her random idiot-savant ability to sway the audience and their buy-in to her story as envisioned and perpetrated by Peeta. If Peeta hadn't been in love with her and spun the tale of that love, she likely would have been voted off the island. She's the girl version of Theseus thrust into the labyrinth dependent on Peeta-Ariadne's golden-thread to find her way back out. She's the sweet girl everyone wanted the Bachelor to pick, the quirky compassionate under-privileged rags to riches Cinderella that we as story-consumers gorge ourselves on (Are we really any different than the District audiences in the novel? Is it ironic that we vote for team Peeta or team Gale?). Katniss is the quintessential Reality TV star who finishes her Nielsen rating-smashing three series on the show, has her cover on TIME and People, does the interviews with Barbara and Oprah, walks the red carpet, and is so damaged beyond repair by the experience that she retires into reality show winner obscurity somewhere in the Midwest. Someday they'll trot her out for an episode of Where are they Now and One Hit Wonders and ask her "What was it like to be the Mockingjay?" How absolutely horrifying. I bawled at the scene where Buttercup comes home. Just thinking about that scene still makes me tear up. This scene is the ultimate catharsis of the entire trilogy. Like Katniss, Buttercup is a survivor. They both did everything in their power to be with and love Prim unconditionally, and in the end, they're alone with each other. I'm still thinking about this trilogy weeks after reading it and having new thoughts. For me, that makes it well deserving of a 4-5 star rating.

Right around a 4. Of the three books I've read, this was my least favorite. Of course, with a series this entertaining, being the least favorite is in no way an insult. Titan's Curse is still heads and shoulders above many of the books out there today. Plot: When Percy, Annabeth and Thalia go to pick up two new potential campers, Annabeth is kidnapped. Artemis and her hunters begin a quest to rescue Annabeth, and Percy, Grover and Thalia go with them. Along the way, they face several mythical creatures, attacks from the Titan army, and eventually a battle with Luke and one of the Titan leaders. Characters: Percy's greatest gift, which some consider his fatal flaw, is that he will do anything he can to keep the camp safe and protect his friends. As he does, he learns more about what he can do and grows more confident in his ability to use his powers effectively. At the same time, he continues to try and figure out his role in the prophecy about Kronos and the destruction of Olympus. Thalia is faced with the same problem, but she is a little more bitter than Percy about being deserted by her father. Grover is a steadfast and loyal sidekick, as is Annabeth even though we don't see much of her. We also don't see much of Luke in this book either, but when we do, we learn that while he is still malicious, he is growing weaker and more scared of Kronos and his soldiers. There are several new characters. Artemis, the leader of the hunters, initially refuses to work with Percy because he's a boy, but in the end, she respects him because of how he fought for his friends. One of Artemis' hunters, Zoe, also plays a huge role in helping to locate and rescue Annabeth. There are also the two campers, Nico and Bianca, who appeared at the beginning of the story. In the book's conclusion, we learn that one of them could be part of the prophecy as well. Writing: The book is very well edited, which I always love. Another plus is Riordan's writing style, which is very laid back and witty. I have been reading it with my son, and there are times that he and I both laugh out loud at things the characters do or say. There's no foul language, but there is (as to be expected) a lot of violence, though most of it isn't too terribly graphic. I'd probably rate the book a PG. The Bottom Line: In comparison to Lightning Thief or Sea of Monsters, there are a few more lulls in the plot. Even with those lulls, there is plenty of action, drama, humor, mystery, and suspense that make this book well worth the read. Like the previous books, Titan's Curse sends some great messages: 1) even when we don't get along, it is still possible to work together to accomplish something, and 2) family isn't always blood. I'd recommend it to readers of all ages.

Siege and Storm continues the enchanting story of Alina, Mal, and the Darkling, in their world full of danger and secrets. Starting with a bang, we're reacquainted with Alina and Mal trapped in a less than stellar situation on the Darkling's ship. This is sure to immediately captivate any fan of the series, pulling us again in this magic-filled story of the Sun Summoner. It didn't take long until the characters carved their way into my heart again. I wasn't as impressed with this sequel as I was with Shadow and Bone, but the characters are still as charming as ever, and the world building is simply fantastic. In an action packed beginning, we meet a new mysterious character that becomes quite a big part of this sequel. However, I was saddened by how he seemed to replaces the Darkling. He's not an enigma like the Darkling - even though he does give off that vibe quite a bit - nor is he even close to being as charismatic, so sadly it did not compensate for the Darkling being MIA for 90% of this novel. While the latter does make sporadic mysterious appearances, the absence of this mysterious villain was my biggest letdown during this book. His personality and the atmosphere he infused in Shadow and Bone had me equally frustrated and mesmerized, so I felt like I was left with a void. A void I'm thinking this new character was supposed to fill but unfortunately did not quite get there for me. The fact that Mal never made any real connection with me surely did not help either as he is also a large part of this book. I do like his character, but he doesn't exactly do anything for me emotionally or romantically. Nonetheless, as far as characters go, we do get a slew of fantastic secondary characters who don't miss the mark in this sequel. They give the book a lot of personality. There is a large number to keep track of, though; it can take a bit of mental effort to keep everyone straight, especially if it's been a while since reading the first book. After this action packed beginning at sea, we revisit this monster-filled world full of war and magic. I loved learning more of the world, especially more about Alina's powers and what she is trying to become. I was hoping for more actual plot progress, however. The placing slows to a crawl mid-book, switching to a relationship and character heavy novel. It's great to see Alina come into herself, figuring out who she is, who she needs to be, but I would be lying if I said this was very exciting. As much as I love character development, I found myself restless with the lack of action. High fantasy is a genre that is a bit out of my comfort zone, though - I was even surprised by how much I loved the first book - so I'm convinced that those with a passion for fantasy won't mind this at all. It begins with a bang, and it ends with one as well. The ending finally brings us back the Darkling (yehaw!) for an exciting and action filled climax. I loved how bold it was, as well as how serious it quickly became. Death and emotion are not missing from it, neither is the promise of an exciting conclusion in the third book. As I said, this genre is a hard sell for me, the first novel's action packed plot reeled me in; the loss of magic in this sequel is due to a personal taste rather than a reflection on the book itself. Leigh is an incredible writer and I have no doubt she will catch the hearts of all fantasy lovers yet again! -- An advance copy was provided by the publisher for review. Wow! This was an amazing read. It's hard to write up a brief summary of what this book is about because there was so much going on. It opens with bodies falling, bullets flying and it doesn't stop there. I've read a lot of science fiction novels and I have to say this is one of my favorites. So much blood was shed during the course of this book as the world of Frihet rebelled against Earth. Earth's only chance for victory is the alien ship Spearhead, run by Joniskyredread, a Sklalen, who we refer to simply as Jon, and his human friend, Bryant Johnson. There are a lot of characters throughout this book and they all seem to pop out from the pages. There are obvious evil ones, good ones and the ones we don't know whether or not we can trust. No matter which side they're on, the characters are to be remembered. In reference to Jon, though, I sometimes had a hard time keeping in mind that he was an alien. We're reminded of his gray skin now and again; however, being referred to as Jon throughout most of the book just made him seem human. The writing was tight and well done. I almost heard the war going on within the safety of my own home. My biggest issue was the POV. I noticed it especially toward the ending that we're in one character's POV and suddenly we know what the other is thinking or feeling. I don't think it happened too often earlier on but it's possible I overlooked it because I was too engrossed in the tale. It's also possible it was meant to be that way in order to help the speedy pace. Either way, I prefer to focus on one person's mind. Additionally, what really gnawed at me were the use of characters' thoughts. I like it when authors italicize the thinking so it's kept separate from the narration. This author didn't do that. There were a lot of times when it's a lone sentence in a paragraph, making it first person. After that one sentence, the narration would continue a new paragraph in its usual third person, until a short paragraph later, it's back with a lone sentence in the first. It just struck me as awkward. But still, I rate this book as amazing. I feel any science fiction fan or any war lovers would enjoy this book. It's a thrill ride you need to buckle up for. *For more book reviews, visit https://angelakaysbooks.com/book-revi...*

Having spent some time in Asia teaching English, I had an unexpectedly large amount of overlapping experience to Kim in this book. Granted, my students were the rural poor of the (comparatively) open China, and not the elite of a despotic murderous gangster-cult of North Korea. But there was a lot that rang true when it comes to bonding with, and being both delighted and befuddled by, classrooms full of students from a different culture. That part of the book was great, even if Kim seemed to squeeze 100+ pages of drama and pathos out of a fleetingly brief summer semester. Where this book really fell down for me was how limited the scope was seen looking at North Korea as a whole. Kim clearly has the experience and background to give us a lot more about this country and its path from the Korean War and into the 21st century. But she tacks pretty close to being mostly pure memoir here; a shame, because she could easily reach out beyond the gates of PUST and tell us a lot more about the country as a whole. That she doesn't, even after making a career from working with escapees and others working to clean up after North Korea, is just a shame and a missed opportunity. As a memoir concerned with a tiny slice of life in North Korea this is a solid B+. But as a book that tells me about North Korea, it comes up short. Much like her students and her time at PUST, if only Kim could look beyond the confines of that campus and tell us more about this bizarre land of North Korea ...

Los Angeles, the city of angels, is full of ex-spooks. Former secret government agents who've done, and had done to them, terrible things and are now living out their early retirement years in LA - unable to leave. Jones is one such ex-spook, a survivor of the mysterious Desolation Project in England, who also freelances as a covert detective. A wealthy old man contacts him to recover a precious item: a reel of secret home-made porn by Adolf Hitler himself, filmed in his bunker! But as Jones is about to discover, the Hitler porn is the red herring in a case that becomes more complicated by the hour as several people begin gunning for him! Desolation Jones is basically Warren Ellis writing his version of Raymond Chandler's LA Noir stories. The pieces are all there: the world-weary detective with the shady past, running from something horrible via intoxicants; the femme fatale, the employer, the job, the crooks, the underworld businesses and rackets. It's written in Ellis' signature grumpy/sarcastic/witty style where the characters' dialogue is biting and funny, and I loved that. Chandler and noir in general though is not my bag and that's why I found the comic overall kinda average. It's your usual gumshoe stuff, usual tropes, same beats, even down to the bait and switch at the end, and you either enjoy that genre stuff or you don't; I'm in the latter. That's not to say Desolation Jones isn't any good - it's definitely got its moments. The biggest draw, even over Ellis' writing, is JH Williams III's incredible art. If you're reading Sandman: Overture or have read the Batwoman comics he drew, you'll know his art style is insanely imaginative. Same applies to Jones whose story utilises Williams' skills perfectly. We have watery/murky flashbacks, fantastically framed fight choreography, warm, even glorious, hallucinations (Jones' mind is fucked) of angels here and there, and warped, druggy sequences to rival Ralph Steadman. If you're a fan of the artist like me, this is a must-read comic purely for the art. What's surprising in the script is the sober look at the modern porn industry in a scene that sneaks up at you right in the middle of the book. It's realistic, humanises the women involved, convincing, dark, unpleasant and moving all at once - a stark contrast to the jovial madness that makes up most of the book. Transmetropolitan had moments like that and so does Desolation Jones and it's that unpredictable quality to switch gears suddenly is what I love about Ellis' scripts. It's a shame it didn't become a series but I doubt Williams could've maintained the pace given the painstakingly high quality of his work, and it's not a bad standalone book anyway. The plot's a bit same-y for me to totally love but if you're a noir fan, Ellis' homage to Chandler's stories will be right up your alley. Desolation Jones is a fine, disturbed modern equivalent for Philip Marlowe.

"Tales From Out There" is an account about the Barkley Marathons that are arguably the toughest footrace in the world. I have recently become interested in these types of races, but I don't desire to run one. Furtaw's account is something that I am definitely interested in. The Barkleys don't entice me at all, except that I'd love to be there just to witness the race. As for the book, it is mostly a documentary that Ed Furtaw put together about a race that was created and managed by Gary Lazarus Cantrell. While this book is mostly a report as the majority of the chapters are arranged following each race year-by-year through 2009, it is at the same time very whimsical. Chapter 30 captures what Furtaw really believes about the race: "Hopefully the reader has perceived by now that the Barkley Marathons is a special event. It is out there on the edge of possibility. The great majority of attempts to run the Barkley end in failure in the sense of the runner not completing the completing the full five-loop distance. However, those few attempts that end in success are tremendous accomplishments of human endurance. Only the most fit and dedicated endurance athletes have attained this accomplishment...Barkley Training is when we push ourselves to extreme limits to try to get tougher and stronger. Barkley Training is when we accept seemingly meaningless harsh conditions and find meaning in it, because it helps us accept the difficulty and hardships that we know we will face during the Barkley. It pushes us to extend ourselves toward unreachable goals. In this way, the Barkley helps us to be happy with what we can do, even though we cannot do everything toward which we struggle." In essence, the book takes us through the creation and history of an ultra-marathon called the Barkley Marathons. It is a race in the mountains of Frozen Head Park in Tennessee that have evolved into a 5 loop, 20 "Barkley Miles"/loop, 100 mile race that is to be completed within 60 hours. It is grueling only lending itself to 1% finishing rate at the time of this book. One of the most helpful portions of this book is the map on page 8 and the chart on page 9 that is repeatedly referred to throughout the course of the documentary. The best part of the book is the personal nature from which Frozen Ed Furtaw writes as one of the participants. No one reads this book because it is a masterpiece of modern literature, rather one reads this because there is a mythical quality that comes with this endurance race and Furtaw's report does not take away from the legend, but only enhances it. On page 166 he records another racer: "In the end [a reporter] had captured what she came to find: the real Barkley, the greatest race among men and mountains. The real Barkley doesn't end in victory. Its rare finishers are what statisticians call 'outliers.' The real Barkley chases down its strong talen, its brightest stars, and annihilates them. It never ends the way it should. That is the real thing." This book made me want to witness the race not as a racer but through the environment if anything because it would be fun to watch and talk with the sinister creator, Gary Cantrell. It's a good story that encompasses many shorter stories. The race tests the limitations of mankind both physically and psychologically. I'd like to see that kind of human feat. Its a heckuva thing to watch man take on something for which he knows he will fail. I recommend this book because it inspires and its just a grand story.

What is the value of brokenness? Not a one of us wants it. But Jim does a great job of showing how brokenness can be a means of personal transformation, especially for those who are in Christ. God is the master at taking what is broken and making it whole; it is his way. Jim explores the mystery surrounding how God uses pain and loss by examining certain words essential to our faith--12 words in all. Jim shows how these words, when properly understood, bring us into awareness of God's purposes and our ultimate good. The lessons for each word use various scriptures and poses great questions, and these lessons would work well for group study or for personal refection. The material is written with a pastor's heart (though I have no idea if Jim is a pastor). He approaches pain and loss with compassion and warmth. Through these studies, he brings clarity to often misunderstood dimensions of the faith, especially as they relate to pain and hardship. For instance, I found his perspective on the fear of God to be encouraging and refreshing. Overall, this book is well written and uplifting--just what a person needs when dealing with loss and brokenness. For anyone wondering if the pieces of life can be put back together, this is a great resource. I'm pleased to recommend it.

I was fortunate enough to serve as a beta reader for this prequel to Johnson's previous work, Well-Oiled. Cyberbully Blues expands futuristic Mayberry, making it seem more vivid than before. Like its predecessor, this Mayberry Mystery is also more concerned with action than characters, putting it firmly in the category of popular fiction. This book focuses on Dakota "Kodi" Hamilton's life leading up to the events in Well-Oiled. Shy and bookish, Kodi uses her high school experience to broaden her horizons. She embraces athletics, math, and her untapped potential in computer science. Perhaps most importantly, she learns to stand up for herself when faced with bullies, first in cyberspace, then in real life. It is gratifying that Johnson has created a teenage heroine whose interests transcend shopping and dating without having to inhabit a futuristic dystopia (See: The Hunger Games). Kodi Hamilton's choice to deal with her problems by bettering herself instead of nursing a persecution complex makes her a positive role model for kids of either gender and any age. While reading this book, I was overwhelmed with gratitude that I completed my own adolescence before the advent of social media. Johnson's ability to make hypothetical technology from house bots the holos seem commonplace is perhaps his greatest strength. I would not be surprised if similar products appeared on the market by the end of the next decade and I am really, really glad that I will be dealing with them as an adult, not a kid. Parents should be aware that Cyberbully Blues does contain some sexual and violent content including some violent sexual content , but I don't think it's anything teens these days aren't aware of.

Buried Alive in the Blues by J. Daniel Sawyer (M/F and M/M): More than an apocalyptic futuristic short story, this was almost an horror. While the world is crashing down around her, a woman is mourning the loss of her beloved husband Juno. For her nothing matter now, if not the blues, and when the last band in the world playing the right blues comes to town, that is the only reason why she will leave her home. But she is not going only to listen to music and dance, she is going to the end of the world and back again, and through sex she will take her vengeance, or maybe even grant peace to her enemies. Expiry Date by Elizabeth Coldwell (M/F): in its macabre tone, this was probably the most funny of the short stories. Holly has no money to pay for her chip to be upgraded, and at the end of the day she will be dead. She decides that she will enjoy her last day, even if this will mean to cheat her best friend: Suzi has the best husband around, Marco, and Holly wants a piece of him before the end. It's not really cheating since she will be not around to continue to do so. But destiny has other plans. Darkest Night by Elizabeth Schechter (M/M and M/F): for once the M/M pair was not the good one. Moira is an AI of Tariq's spaceshift, and she is always there for him, despite all the different lovers, males and females, entering his life. Now Tariq has Marcus, and he seems happy; Moira has no jealousy in her, and she only wants the best for Tariq, so she doesn't understand why Marcus is so contrary to her. Then Moira intercept a message: the end of the world, know and unknow is coming, and they have only two choice, searching shelter deep in the ground or chosing to die in the space, like they have always lived. Tariq has no doubt, and Moira can only follow what Tariq wants, but Marcus has a slightly different idea. Invasion! by Beverly Langland (F/F and M/F): this is almost a joke, when the radio airs the announce that there is an Invasion from Mars, two women and a man decide that if they have to die, at least they will enjoy the waiting... Fences by David Hubbard (M/M): without doubt Fences was the most romantic and in a way the only one with a bit of hope in the end. Jeremy had a perfect life, a loving husband, a beautiful house in the suburbs, two dogs... the full package, until a lethal virus destroyed everything. Now a widower with his days counted, Jeremy is only waiting for the end, and trying to enjoy what remains of his life. He is not expecting a second chance, above all not to love, but his neighboor, Bradley, is alone as Jeremy, and he has lost everything like Jeremy. Bradley was not gay, and in a normal situation nothing between them could have happened, but this is not a normal situation, and sincerely, now it's more important that you are able to find someone, than being selective on his gender. But even if maybe Jeremy and Bradley get together out of loneliness, it's not a desperate move: both Jeremy than Bradley had a good life before, and they would have been able to live out of their memories, but they don't want to face the end alone. http://www.amazon.com/dp/B003QP4F0W/?...

Masquerade is another great installment to Felicity Heaton's Vampire Realm series. This is book 10 in the series, but it is easily read as a stand alone. Heaton writes all of the books in this series where they can be read as stand alone books or out of order without leaving the confused or feeling like they've missed anything. The world she creates in this series is vividly painted in each book with enough insight that the reader can feel as if they're sitting in the front row watching the show no matter which book they're reading, but without too much fluff or unnecessary detail to make them feeling as if they are drowning in detail. For followers of the series, as always Heaton gives you a peek at previous characters and how they've grown, moved along in the vampire realm world and are doing. Masquerade in particular is a nice treat for this with the Creator Day ball nearing and all of the bloodlines gathering. In this book you'll get snippets from Valentine (yummy), Prophecy, Winter, and (yay) Hyperion (sigh...)! You'll even get a visit from our ware wolf friends. This installment focuses on Vivek & Sophis with and underlying plot with the Hunters back and in full swing trying to strike their vampire targets again. Both characters are strong well defined characters that I found myself thoroughly wrapped up in within a few chapters. Viveck is a strong warrior who uses coldness and cruelty as his shield and comes across as a reall jerk at first, but as I dove into the story I became more and more fascinated with him. Sophis is a bit reckless but an excellent warrior. I found myself living them both quickly and wanting to choke them often. They are both guards for their bloodline. At one time they were very close, but a near death experience changed their relationship. Now it seems as if Vivek is dead set on trying to disgrace Sophis in her position as a guard and get her relieved of her duties, and Sophis is determined to prove herself and show how good a warrior she is to everyone. They are forced to work together to save all the bloodlines when it's learned that the hunters are up to no good again and planning to use the upcoming ball as a means to destroy the vampires since all of the bloodlines will be gathered for the Creator's Day ball. I don't like to tell to much about the books I review so that's enough of that. I will say these vamps are not the nice, fluffy, sparkly, goody goody type vamps you see so much of now days. These vamps are more along the lines of the older style dark, dangerous and deadly vamps. I love them! And, I love the way Heaton draws this world and makes me feel as if I'm there with them in each book! The tension between the two characters had me really wanting to jump into the book and smack them both silly. Granted they'd both kick my butt, but Heaton's style drags me into the story so much it's like yelling at the television while watching your favorite sports team. You just can't help but get personally involved! And when the passion between them does finally explode and the tension is released its one hot, sexy scene. This fast-paced, hot and sexy story with a sweet romance will keep you guessing throughout the plot and may even surprise you with the ending. It's a absolute recommend for me for anyone looking for a paranormal romance that visits the dark and bloody side with a fast pace and hot, sexy scenes. 5 stars

The writing style in The Tidal Zone is amazing... mind blowing. The themes are heavy (death, illness, loss, mortality) but incredibly well translated into a story, not making them feel as heavy as they are. I couldn't stop marking beautiful quotes in the book. One of the best books I've read this year, if not ever. "Ok, all right, phrases to which we cling, the comfort blankets or blindfolds of our time and place. There is no pre-twentieth-century version of 'OK', which may or may not tell us that it is a modern delusion that normality is not frightening, that it is normal not to be frightened. I personally don't like depressing subjects, people say, as if mortality is a lifestyle choice, disease and violence and sorrow a matter of taste."
Excellent journalism. An important look at the technology obsessed culture we all live in. This book answers a difficult question - why do people still text and drive if they know the dangers?
I'd actually give it 3 1/2 stars if it gave me that choice. I am enjoying this series, but it runs hot and cold.

A fascinating and poignant telling of the author's journey around the world by the most dangerous travel routes. The author does an excellent job of making the story about the human experiences of those traveling by the same routes. He also manages to still describing enough of the planes, trains, buses & boats to give the reader an idea how unpleasant this sort of travel can be, without turning it into a horror show.

This is not Miller's best work. What was most interesting to me about this work is that he points out how much time we spend judging other people. Also, he makes the observation that many Christians have narrowed Christianity down to accepting propositions of theology instead of accepting a relationship. I will probably continue to ponder those two ideas, but the rest of the book, meh. Romeo and Juliet -- rolling my eyes. I recommend Blue Like Jazz or What I Learned While Editing My Life as far superior.
I love Miss Marple.
The lyrics of the well-known spiritual are set against stunning pencil, oil, and watercolor artwork. PreK-2.

I liked this book much more than I expected to. Normally when something is labeled romantic suspense, it tends to focus more on the romance and the mystery often isn't really a mystery. With this book, the suspense built slowly, sometimes almost too slowly. I think this was intentional, though, to make you care about the characters and what happened to them, then add a clue to the mystery. The thoughts of the main character, Maisey, are scattered - but rightly so. She has had a complete upheaval in her life and she's reeling. Returning home should have been a comfort to her, but instead, she keeps getting hit with one thing after another. The wrap up was a little clean, but since this is the first book in a series, I hope that leads to more exploration of that and hopefully it isn't as "tied up with a neat little bow" as it seems!
Loved all Ilana Tan's book!!

Another really good read. This was my 2nd by this author. One of the things that pressed on me while I was reading this is that we all have these preconceived notions about who our grandparents are because we carry those ideas with us from childhood. It's when we're grown that we find out there's so much more to them! Love this book! I read this book the day after Suanne's Diary to Nicholas. Again, in a day. Easy reading and I'd read it again.

Angelina is a naive and inexperienced character who does eventually come into her own. Her backstory is an interesting one though and gives good insight into her character and Bardan weaves this through the story seamlessly. Haithem on the other hand... well he is pretty much her exact opposite! He's the quintessential tall, dark, handsome, and devilishly sexy millionaire who is just mysterious enough to be interesting but not so much so that you feel like he's difficult to get to 'know'. The setting, aboard a luxury yacht, lends itself nicely to Angelina and Haithem's insta-lust relationship and certainly offered them a great opportunity to explore the chemistry between them in a very intense way. Suspense and sexiness mixed with luxury and lust makes Didn't I Warn You a great read. Be warned though you'll probably start and finish this novel in one sitting so clear your schedule and settle in!

1842 - A freed slave makes her way to the Oregon Territories. Encountering both kindness and prejudice, Letitia holds true to her values and learns to fit into a land that is against her much of the time. A touching story.

Cutoff dates. They exist, we know that. But who knew that those arbitrary cutoff dates influence learning in the classroom or the performance of hockey players? In the midst of my strangely-scholarly-statistical readings on typically thought to be immeasurable things, the patterns of successful people are amazingly interesting and eye-opening to the point oh "Oh, that makes sense!". Though there are always exceptions, but seeing the links in everything from elementary school learning to pilots to professional hockey players, is downright fascinating.
Super read I love history stories about real people. Interesting descriptors of both ship captains. Reaffirmed my belief to never get on a boat. Upside down life jackets, unbelievably sad.

This guide aims to help people build trusting relationships using stories, some of which are very cheesy. I think the ideas presented are important and young people would especially benefit from reading this book; however, the cheesy-factor will be a big turn off. I would suggest parents read this book and find a way to pass the information on to their kids. As for adults with trust issues...this is probably not the book they will pick up (unfortunately).

THIS. BOOK. OMG. Okay, but seriously, the experience of reading this book has left me feeling as though my heart was ripped out, spun around, and reinstalled. Were it not for time constraints, I might've been dragged full-bodied through the text as though spelled. Much like Luthe's Summoning, actually. Fortunately for me, this one doesn't collapse if you stop reading halfway through. As a fan of the Temeraire series, I couldn't help but tally comparisons. Where the series can be somewhat dry or long-winded, Uprooted is warm and flowing. Both certainly do not spare feelings when it comes to death, but while the former's main character is logical and eloquent, the latter's description of magic comes right from the gut. In fact, her learning sessions remind me of frustrating tutoring in math class, a subject I had aptitude for, but could not process like my teachers. This book will scare you, delight you, break your heart, and cover you in a warm blanket while you recuperate. Read it.

Chilling and beautifully written. I can't say this is one of my favorite books of all time, but it certainly deserves 5 stars for the brilliant writing. Read this one (!) sentence as an example: "Monstrous as it was, the corpse itself seemed little more than a prop, something brought out in the dark by stagehands and laid at Henry's feet, to be discovered when the lights came up; the picture of it, staring and dumb in all its gore, never failed to provoke an anxious little frisson but still it seemed relatively harmless compared to the very real and persistent menace which I now saw that Bunny presented."

I actually had read all the rest of the B.A.D. series before I went back and read this first installment. If I had started with Bad Attitude, I probably would have liked it much better. It was fast paced and, of course, steamy but not as exciting as the other books where Kenyon collaborated with Dianna Love. The plot and action sequences were exciting (a little far fetched) and the connection between Sydney and Steele was intense. The ending twist was disappointing. I couldn't help but wish that the confrontation that everyone expected to occur would have taken place. Other then that, a good start to the series. I am dying, and crossing my fingers for, an installment that revolves around Joe and Tee.
One of the worst books I have ever read.

Absolutely loved it, a must read for movie buffs! This book has inspired me to start a Bad Movies Viewing club! My only complaints are that one, I didn't write this book first, and two, the work of Joan Crawford appears here way too many times!

The introduction assures us that, "Every project is totally different," but from what? I'm not sure. I agree that it is: "from the outset an unknown voyage of discovery...it's left to us to explore each path to its natural creative end." And great fun it was, too. I must admit though, that if I were a beginner without a trusty guide, this would likely be a voyage to frustration. There are a few changes that I would make to adapt them to my liking (which I explain). This collection is intended for joy: Giving is a celebration in itself, and sometimes all we need is a good excuse: "Births, engagements, weddings, namings, housewarmings, anniversaries, even funerals--celebrate a life and help us remember all the things we love about a person. Gatherings and parties remind us of the good things in life and give a sense of perspective to the difficult times. Giving makes you feel good, and this feeling of well being allows you to relax and regenerate, opening up new possibilities for the future." The first piece I tested was the Odalisque Turban on pages 66-68. I love vintage clothing, and this is a classic Rosie the Riveter working girl's hair wrap. Knitted in Brioche Stitch, several variations are possible: from one single color to four (or even more), and you can stop with just a headband, or work the top to make it a hat. My started as a headband, but I found the stretch too loose to keep my hair under control. It's now a warm, lightweight, not washing my hair today cap. A new hairband in the smaller size won't take long to work up. Next, my adaptation of the Hendrix Guitar Strap (pages 89-90) is psychedelic and speedy. As a camera strap, I only needed to work 55 cm without buttonholes, seaming right over the original manufactured strap. I recommend not slipping the 1st st of each row. The mattress stitch looks much tidier when I can pick up every ladder of the seam. In addition, instead of working the back half of the strap in stockinette, seed stitch would be a bit more stable and equitable to the cable pattern gauge. The Knot Stitch Cable looks great in two tones. One other change I'd make is to use 1 less stitch on the cable piece; as the cable is worked over a multiple of 16 sts, only 1 st is required at the start of the row for seaming. The opposite selvedge is superfluous next to the Contrast Color backing. You can see on the photo that the top edge of the cable stands out better than the lower edge because of that extra plain stitch. Finally, a fun way to dabble in eccentric yarns! Remember the early 2000s, when faux fur fantasy scarves were the rage? My daughters couldn't get enough of the stuff. Okay, so it doesn't show off the Wensleydale Tea Cosy (pp. 105-107) to its best advantage, but I really like how the Tuck-Stitch Pattern creates thermal baffles in the fabric. I intend to make this pattern again, and I won't change a thing, except to back off on the outrageous yarns a bit...maybe... The Contents Include: Introduction Chapter 1: Baby (Cuddle Cocoon, Shower Set, Baby Love Blanket, Whoopla Beanbags, Jubilee Jacket and Hat) Chapter 2: Hers (Fiesta Shrug and Fingerless Gloves, Jive Leg Warmers, Glow Wristlets, Froufrou Fingerless Gloves, Amulet Purse, Deco Backpack, Will-o'-the-Wisp Shawlette, Galaxy Beret, Kitten's Paw Stole, Odalisque Turban and Hat, Zebra Mittens) Chapter 3: His (Hugs Socks, Masham Scarf, Galway Beanie and Head Wrap, Tutti-Frutti Smartphone Sleeve, Hendrix Guitar Strap and Linen Belt) Chapter 4: Home (Checkers Cushion and Seat Cover, Flavor Place Mat and Napkin Ring, Wensleydale Tea Cozy, McDougal Dog Jacket, Welcome Toran Door Hanging) Appendices: Techniques and Stitches, Yarn Information, Buttons and Trimmings, Knitting Abbreviations, Needle and Hook Sizing, Project Index, Index, About the Author. Jean Moss is self-taught Britain knitwear designer who employs evocative combinations of intricate textures, striking color ways, and sophisticated styling. Passionate about good design, Jean believes that it should be available to all who appreciate it, not just the few who can afford to buy couture. Great Little Gifts to Knit is her 11th book of handknit designs, the most recent being Sweet Shawlettes (The Taunton Press). Currently, her designs are featured regularly in Rowan Knitting and Crochet magazine, The Knitter, and Vogue Knitting, and for six years she hosted "Ask Jean," an advice column in the U.K. magazine Knitting. Also in About the Author, I learned that, "For the past decade, Jean and her partner, Philip, have hosted knitting and garden tours in the United Kingdom, which have become so successful that they are now going further afield to exotic locations such as Morocco and Greece. She loves to meet other knitters and travels extensively, teaching workshops in both the United States and Europe. For more information on Jean's books, patterns, kits, ready-to-wear, workshops, lectures, and tours, visit www.jeanmoss.com." So, I hope she'll consider making knitting visit to Provence ;0)

What I most enjoyed about this book was trying to figure out which character was Dave Barry and which was Alan Zweibel. This was a completely silly book, but definitely fun to read. It really reminded me of sitting in HS classrooms writing hidden-sentence stories (you know - where you write one sentence on lined paper leaving one word hanging on the next line, then you fold the paper over so that the kid you pass the paper to can only see the one word and has to continue the story from there knowing nothing but the one word.)

Gemma had a perfect life before going to the airport with her parents, from going to get coffee across the boarding area her life changed into being the missing girl from England. A mysterious guy named Ty, finds the girl from his dreams and steals her from her world throwing her into his world full of silence, heat and empty, barren lands. This book was a struggle, what I mean by a struggle was I mentally died, and it was a completely different and such an original book from what I've ever read before. It was a rollercoaster of immediate feelings of love, hurt, hatred, with so many other feelings that I currently can't name. Lucy Christopher, a master mind of words, created the most interesting captor matching with a strong female lead. Stolen is full of pointless escape attempts, enjoyable banters and heart-breaking moments. The two main characters in this novel have played a huge role in creating a real life heart-breaking story about a girl being kidnapped and trapped in a place with no escape from an emotionally unstable captor. Ty, who was the captor, had a rich history of being hurt, misused, and neglected. All of these experiences have made Ty a lonely, detrimental time bomb, who loves easily while getting hurt all of the time. He's such a sweetie to Gemma, by helping her, feeding her while trying his best to please her. But while Ty is a good kind person, he made an awful mistake of taking someone against their will and a moral mistake of trying to make someone love him back. While Ty was the captor, Gemma was the victim, and was mostly an interesting character. At some point in the book I felt that she became depressed and lonely and basically lost her fight in her and succumbed into being trapped. I loved the character especially when she started seeing that Ty only loved her and started to return his love back. Maybe its messed up for me to say this but I felt these two characters were meant for each other. "What you did to me wasn't this brilliant thing, like you think it was. You took me away from everything- my parents, my friends, my life. You took me to the sand and the heat, the dirt and isolation. And you expected me to love you." This quote basically explains the whole book of him hoping and praying that someday she would be okay from being in isolation away from society. He did sort of have a good plan but the one thing wrong was he took something that wasn't for him to take. The truth was that, he was wrong to take her to Australia and to expect her to love him. This book was the hardest and most amazing book I've read in a while and it made me cry and wish that everything was different for her and him. It was super hard to get through with not crying for them and an unemotional person would probably be the only one person that wouldn't cry. I give this book a 5 star rating because this story was original, beautiful and was full of a passionate, heart-breaking romance. I totally recommend this book to everyone to read because once you do read it, you won't be able to stop reading the book while not being able to not cry. So this book was amazing and Lucy Christopher has made me into an emotional sap over this book. So, I love you guys and wish you the best for reading any book you desire. http://slayerofya.wordpress.com/?p=67...

So excellent! I loved the first book, but this was a lot more fun. Larks character is quirky and tough, and Simon was totally hot. The character chemistry was really good, and the story was great. This series is a must read.
Loved this book. The end really gets ya.

I have previously read other books by Kate Morton which is why I picked up this book. True to her style, the book keeps you guessing and waiting for the next twist she'll throw your way. She has successfully evoked the feeling of mystery and macabre in the reader and makes you feel along with the central characters, their loneliness, sadness and helplessness. However, my complaint with the book is the lengthy descriptions which sometimes appear to be unnecessary. As always, her book, once finished, makes me want to take some time off reading to let the story, the characters, the emotions sink in.
It's solid. Just not as strong as the others. I do dig Princess Leia finally getting her spotlight, though!

I think this was bya far my favourite one of the series. It went a lot quicker than the other books. I liked that the setting and the storylines moved around quite a bit keeping the reader intrigued. I however think it's in a good place to end the series. That being said if another book comes up I will probably read it.

I'd give this 3.5 stars though I'm surprised it doesn't have a higher rating here. I'm unusually picky about a few things and this book really had me on one of them or I would have rated this much higher. It's almost 500 pages which is great but it didn't really take me much longer to read than a normal regency romance. I do feel that it has 2 distinct parts before London and in London and I would have loved to seen a "Part 1" and "Part 2" in this novel. That's where I really think a better editor would have been handy along with cutting out one or two scenes that seems to take away from the book instead of add to it. Since it happens withing the first few pages I don't consider it a spoiler that the heroine's father is both physically and mentally/emotionally abusive and has been since she was about 3 when her mother died. Her inattentive husband, while not physically abusive to her is uncaring and emotionally/mentally abusive. I think this is a big point, though while focused on as why she has a hard time trusting men, the author fails over and over to really show what a victim of this kind of abuse for over 20 years needs in a partner. I really wanted to love Sion, and I think he is a good hero, but a few times knowing her past he rubbed me the wrong way. Once time he physically put his hands on her when he was angry with her (for a reason he shouldn't have been) not only did he scare her but he also hurt her which she voiced and he wouldn't let go. This points to signs of an abusive relationship as well though from reading the book it's easy to tell that is not what the author is going for. She wants them to have "tension" or "chemistry" it just missed the mark which is why I had to mark it as a book needing trigger warnings. There is another point where he locks her in her room, (mind you they are not married, she is still married to another man, and is trying to get her inheritance so she can be independent) and a few other things that point to cutting her off, blaming her for making him angry, and other key signs of an abusive relationship. Again I really don't think this is what the author is trying to do, she just need a better editor or more research into growing up with abuse and how those people processes it as adults and what kind of support they need. The points I did love were the plot. It was such a unique idea and I loved it, I just wished it had been pulled off a little better so I could have given it just a little better rating. The length. I love reading a good long book when it's well written. It's well written even with the few flaws in the editing and the abuse angle. Over all it was enjoyable and I would recommend it, like I said I just have a few things I'm extra picky about (grammar, continuity, abusive H or h/doormat h or H) and this one just hit on one of those so I had to knock it down a star. I would read this author again.

There were some interesting things in this book, and I enjoyed going back and forth between the perspectives of the psychically linked brother and sister. The dystopian society set up here is interesting as well. And I did enjoy the video game-training portion. Overall though, I felt this was pretty run of the mill. And I think I knew exactly what was going on beyond the wall from the first time the wall was mentioned. The writing was very simple, and many of the characters were very one dimensional. However, the action moved quickly and made the book enjoyable.

I'm seriously addicted to these novella collections. I love reading them in between longer books and especially on busy days to get a quick fix. I enjoyed all these stories equally and the California setting was definitely close to home! The first one by Heather Moore was even set at a beach we go to frequently throughout the year and especially in the summer. It is impressive that the characters and plot are introduced quickly but in a way that doesn't feel rushed. It was easy to connect with the emotions of the main characters and even though the stories are often wrapped up before I'm ready for them to end, they are a pleasure to escape with :) (Thank you to Ebooks For Review for a copy of the book in exchange for my honest review)
Very well written.
I prefer 'crash into you' than 'devil in black jeans'. But, it's nice.

Not as gripping as the first two Ophelia and Abby mysteries. In fact, I thought the storyline was a bit boring. It wasn't very exciting, moved slow, and I am glad it's finally over. I'm not sure what the next book will be like with the addition of Tink to the mix.

Positives: The premise was great! I loved how the author wove together ancient history with a modern apocalypse story. Her writing style was very engaging and I didn't want to put the book down! Negative: I didn't like the font used on the cover.

This was definitely an interesting concept, but it fell kind of flat in some parts. I love the twist on imaginary friends, especially since I had one of my own as a child. I'm not sure if it was the writing style or what, but despite the interesting storyline I found myself bored in quite a few spots.
This book was awesome but so sad at the same time ...really interested to get a peek into frostys head in the next book :)

Dust City was not my favorite fairy tale retelling, not by a long shot. I'd much rather had reread any of Alex Flinn's books. But, the book wasn't horrible. It was simply okay. There were a few scenes and chapters that I really enjoyed but they weren't enough for me to really like this book. In the world of Dust City, fairydust is a drug. It can do anything, from a concussion to raising the dead. Everyone uses it and it's very addicting. But the fairies aren't the ones with the dust. The fairies disappeared when Henry was a pup and now a corporation called Nimbus is distributing the dust. Henry breaks out of his wayward house to try to find out why the fairies left, if his dad is innocent and where Nimbus gets their dust. He meets a whole cast of characters, many of them with their own traditional fairy tale background. For example, Jack; Jack and the Bean stock; Detective White, Snow White; Skinner, Midas; Cindy Bella, Cinderella; among others. One of the major problems for me was picturing the animalia. In Dust City, many species of animals have evolved to stand up right, were clothes and talk. Also, these animals are the size of humans. That means there are wolves, frogs, ravens, and foxes walking around as big as you and me. This was incredibly hard to picture. I pictured Henry and Fiona as humans all of the time. On the character side of things, I thought the main characters could have been better. They were a little flat. I like the side characters much more, even the ones who are supposed to be Henry's nemesis. My favorite characters where Detective White and Tom. What I can say positively is that I never guessed the twists. They always surprised me. Also I LOVED the setting. A city hooked on dust, it's like a city hooked on drugs and what can be more interesting? I especially liked the gritty scenes when Henry was delivering dust to addicts. I thought that seeing how hooked the city was on dust brought the story to a deeper level. However, I felt these parts should have been part of a different book. One that delved deeper into the city's connection to dust, because while Dust City did have these scenes they were never mentioned again and they would have been and should have been dramatizing to Henry. If you have nothing better to read, and you find Dust City on your library shelf, I would say give it a try. While very cheesy throughout most of the book, there are scenes that will make you think and wonder if our society is following the same path. Also Dust City is full of non-stop action with a little wolfy romance slipped it.
This was ok, but I liked the other books way better.

This is book 5 of the Vampire Academy series and in this book Rose Hathaway and her friends have just graduated from St Vladimir's. We get to travel to the Court and meet a few new characters along the way. This book held a lot of surprises for me. None of which I can actually mention but I will just say that you will be shocked at some of the things that happen. This book was in no way predictable for me. Richelle is an amazing writer. Rose is probably one of my favorite characters ever in a book or series. She continues to be strong, outspoken, and dangerous but I feel this book gave her a little more vulnerability. I felt like I really got to know her character a lot more. It was nice for her to be around some of the people that were missing from Blood Promise book 4. She was able to focus on her feelings and show that for once, she may not know what to do. So in conclusion, the setting was great, you really get to experience another side to their already complicated world. The characters continue to be well developed and the new people we meet in this book are really interesting. The plot was...wow! I never knew where this book would turn. In the end I was still completely shocked. Once you read this book you will have no choice but to pick up book 6, Last Sacrifice. Unfortunately, we will have to wait till December to read it.

I had very mixed feelings about this book. As light, fluffy entertainment it was fine, but too many of the characters seemed to undergo major personality shifts between the beginning and the end of the book.

This is the second omniscient narrator book I've read in a few weeks, which is strange since I feel as though they're rare. Maybe not as rare as I'd thought, and, as far as Descent is concerned, I'm glad about that. Johnston weaves a brow-furrowingly tense story using a style that is at times poetic, but at other times withheld. This style mimics his characters' struggles -- and, god, what struggles they are -- and makes each and every word feel purposeful.

The third book in the series didn't disappoint. The pace was fast and exciting. This book could stand on it's own quite easily but reading the other 2 books would definitely put you in the mood for more mystery. Darcy's character received great background build. The only thing that disappointed me was the lack of focus on Gage even though he was the secondary lead in the story, he is part of the McKenna family rather than Darcy but then I guess the series is more about the courage of women. In following the Courage theme Darcy faced many situations where it took her reliance on God to get her to come through the physical and psychological trials. Some of the twists were expected, some were not. All in all a great mystery read.

Not a lot to say about this book. I wasn't that impressed by the short story format. Hattie's twelve children hold a chapter of the book and present different aspects of Hattie after the death of her twins. It was a very poetic story with lines very similar to an African parable. Unfortunately the great writing was a thin veneer for directionless plot and a poorly explored central character. This was not really my type of book. I can't believe I read this shit, the worst book I've read ever

I love how Emily Murphy wasn't looking for love but it found her in the form of Nate Thalberg.. I believe in love and I believe that love will hit me when I least expect it.. but till then I will be just like most of your characters.

"Fear is a strange thing. It has the power to make people close their eyes, turn away. Nothing good grows out of fear." 4.5/5 Lexi knows there's more to her little village of Near than anyone around her seems willing to admit. When a stranger comes to town for the first time in years, and bad things begin to happen, Lexi seizes the opportunity to find out more, and she inevitably gets sucked into a series of dramatic events directly affecting herself, the handsome stranger, and the forces of the moor around Near. I loved this! I devoured it in under 24 hours nearly without noticing how much time was passing me by as I read it. It reminded me of a cross between Hocus Pocus (the film) and Uprooted, with little dashes of concepts Schwab employed in some of her later books (elemental magic, blurred lines between life and death, ...cloaks and knives). I've heard Victoria speak about this book, her first published, as having been difficult to complete. I can see where the effort may have gone in the most: the creases of the plot, the bricks that built up the world, the slightly forced romance (which is where that one .5 went for the rating, although I still rounded up bc I fell for them together anyway). Overall, I liked the world because it was hard to pin down - so real and recognizable yet not quite enough to point out what region or historical period it might have been based upon. In the end, it's a world of magic, where witches come alive and the moor whispers back with an important message about fear to share, so listen.
I knew nothing about the Haitian massacre in the 30's before reading this book. It is similar to the tales of horror told by Rwandan survivors. Mans' inhumanity to man.
Another post apocalyptic book. I liked this one, though. It was different from the others and had me hooked. Would recommend. The relationships were worth reading about.

The Succubus Gift is the first book in The Telepathic Clans series by B.R. Kingsolver. When approached by the author I was very excited to read this book; it sounded like something I'd really enjoy. It sounded like a really different spin on the paranormal. I enjoyed it more than I thought I would and that's saying something. The story follows members of the Clan as they find a family member they thought to be dead and learn about her abilities. I really enjoyed the emphasis on family and loyalty. This is a family you DO NOT want to cross. They're lovely people, of course, but hurt them or one of theirs and you'll wish you were never born. I loved every one of them! I think she could tell the story from any one of their points of view and it would be fantastic. They're all so interesting and well developed; definitely not cookie cutter characters. Brenna is such a kick ass character, I really loved her! She is strong, determined, funny, sexy and honest, a dangerous combination, for sure! I think every woman secretly wishes she could be more like Brenna is. She doesn't shy away from putting herself in danger to protect others. I really loved the dynamics of the friendship between her and Rebecca, her protector. It was very interesting & I hope we learn more about it in the next book. This book had it all; lots of action, romance, suspense and humor. Loaded with intrigue and drama, it was a very fast read! I was on pins and needles for the whole book, almost, waiting to see what would happen next. I really love Kingslover's writing style and I cannot wait for book #2!
One of the better thrillers I've read this year.

I really wanted to like this book because I adore Lauren Graham, but I just couldn't. There was no character development and the plot felt pretty flat. Thinking back on it, I can't remember much of what happened because nothing really happened at all. I wish there was more depth not just with Frannie, but with all of the characters.

I'm at a loss as to how to review this book. It is not what I would call an enjoyable read, but there were aspects of it that I liked and it is thought provoking. It takes place somewhere in the south near the Gulf coast and Warren does an excellent job of describing the area and the time. As far as my experience goes, A Canticle for Leibowitz is utterly unique. It is a work of post-apocalyptic fiction, before there was a genre of that name, whilst being at the same time a discourse on knowledge, religion and morality, and what it means to be truly human. The book is split in to three parts, that offer a defamiliarised exploration of the old and new testaments. The world has been destroyed, probably as the result of the cold war, and man sets out to rebuild it a-new. The trouble is that while some strive to create Eden, others are concerned only with power and the same mistakes are made over, and over again. Miller, in his only novel, has crafted something so well-written and solid that it feels like genuine myth, or the writing of a saint. The tone is perfect. The parched, dry wasteland in which the knowledge of a destroyed post-nuclear age is kept in fragments and hidden from the outside world is up there with some of the best science fiction I've read, and is genuinely very, very good. Miller has a habit of attaching you to his characters, and then hitting you straight between the eyes. I won't go in to details, but you'll see what I mean when you read this. The spiritual foundation for the novel creates a peculiar mix between science and God. The Bible has survived the apocalypse, and faith, if anything, has grown stronger. Yet curiously, the saint about whom this story is told is a man of science. The world that develops on this foundation is a curious symbiosis of religion and secular science that lives and breathes and leaves you feeling at times genuinely hopeful, despairing, confused, bewildered, and befuddled by enigma. I love this book. The only reason I haven't given it a five is that there were some nagging gaps in the story that I personally felt needed exploring more. It was probably Miller's intention to leave us asking who Ben Eleazer really is, but at the same time, I can't help but think that some sort of revelation about him would have been the sucker punch that this book needed to put it up there amongst the greats. Please read it. It's a little obscure, and a little hard to find, but well worth your time!

I found this book to be extremely interesting. It is not just a true crime story (like that of the disappearance of Natalee Holloway, although there are some strong parallels) but a tale of two completely different cultures and how they handle crime, judicial matters and sentences of a perpetrator of a crime. The girl focused on in this book, Lucie Blackman, disappeared on July 1, 2000, and was later found to be the victim of an atrocious crime. However, it took the Japanese justice system at least six years to bring the alleged criminal to trial, and there are still open and very strange questions about the case. What this 21-year old's disappearance did to her family was terrible beyond belief; having to search for her themselves, being stonewalled by the Tokyo Police, etc. It is a fact that the country of Japan has far less serious crime than most other countries. That is one of the reasons why the police department appears to be rather inept. It is also true that there is a certain cultural disdain among some Japanese for foreign citizens, including Koreans (what is what the perpetrator in this story is). Lucie Blackman had gone over to Tokyo with a friend to work as a bar hostess (NOT prostitute, although there are bars that offer those services also). The crime novelist Mo Hayder herself had done this very same job at one time before she started her writing career. The duties of the bar hostess include lighting men's smokes, pouring their drinks, sitting with them and semi-flirting with them with meaningless conversation. The hostesses are also expected to go to lunches or dinners with their clients several times per month, otherwise they are fired. It was poor Ms. Blackman's bad luck to go to lunch with the last person who saw her alive. (He had a history of drugging his companions with Rohypnol, GHB and/or chloroform and five years before this case, he overdosed an Australian woman with chloroform). After he had drugged them, he raped them, all the while filming the whole tawdry scene wearing a ski mask. The author theorizes that the women preyed upon by this guy didn't see any danger in him because he was polite, soft-spoken, etc. That is also a major cultural difference between Japanese men and men of other countries, in general. This particular man had NO friends at all while he grew up (had an IQ of 180) and was basically a loner, and a stranger, himself, in a strange land. The book goes into the history between the war between Korea and Japan and events that occurred because of that. The other interesting note the author brought out is that certain Japanese men look upon blonde (especially) caucasian women as worldly, at the same time rather wanton, but also goddesses. It was very hard for me to get my mind around this concept because it sounds so outlandish in the 21st Century. A very interesting book and definitely worth reading!

Containing neither the slight but otherworldly charms of The Virgin Suicides nor the sprawling (sometimes ungainly) vibrancy of Middlesex it doesn't seem unreasonable to question: who exactly is meant to want to read The Marriage Plot? After all, a story about three really quite privileged Ivy League graduates whining about literature, life and love for over 400 pages doesn't exactly sound like an easy sell, or at least, only to a niche market. I get the feeling that the publisher had this fear too: prominent on my edition is a quote from the Times declaring that this is 'One Day with George Eliot thrown in'... Aha! So this book is meant for people too snooty to admit to reading something as mass market as One Day, but who still long for a little romance in their life. This is rom com for smart people: worry not, for all smooshy bits will be leavened out with copious quoting from Barthes, and there's even mental illness to make us feel deep. Cynicism aside, I should probably offer full disclosure: I think I am exactly the niche market this book is aiming for (English Lit grad & hopeless romantic, reporting for duty!). And yes there is lots to enjoy in this book. The first section in particular is a masterclass in shifting through narrative time. Ostensibly the section is set entirely on the day of Madeleine Hanna's graduation, but effortlessly and seamlessly Eugenides feeds us information about her academic career and interests, her romantic life, her family background. This is all done so lightly that we barely notice it happening - this tight packed density here is Eugenides writing at his best. This first section is full of treats, too, for the lit geek, full to the brim with satire and self-knowing (but affectionate) irony: the cool kids in semiotics class chasing the next big thing, the horror of realising you love totally untrendy books with no smart justification but just because, the lure of reading everything in your own life as if it's something from the books you've been studying... Bookworms, get ready to have a (sometimes uncomfortable) mirror held up to your foibles. Elsewhere in the book Eugenides utilises an interesting narrative technique - a combination of shifting free indirect style between each of his three protagonists, and carefully selected revelations, which become fleshed out in later sections as other characters remember events differently - which establishes a kind of unreliable (and yet still omniscient) third person narrator. The effect is mostly successful, although at times we can read the same event from three (slightly different) perspectives, which begins to feel repetitive, and slows the pace of the novel down. Perhaps this is a contributing factor to the sense that after an initial burst of verve and fizz, the novel begin to unravel - from the densely plotted and rich first section, time begins to telescope and the plot rushes towards its slightly dissatisfying end. However, as I hinted at at the beginning of this review, I don't really think it's a flaw in structure or pacing that is this book's problem. It's something much more central than that: plot and character. The real beauty of both The Virgin Suicides and Middlesex is that they took worlds and narratives (suburban America, the immigrant experience) that felt familiar, and then exposed their dark unsettling undersides, made us see them in a new light or from new perspectives. And for a book that explicitly sets ties itself to a literary theory (the marriage plot that powers the vast majority of 19th C fiction) Eugenides implies that he will have something new to bring to the table on this front, too. Unfortunately, in spite of the mental illness, the homosexual experimentation, the sex, the college feminists - all the things that are trying to take us away from conventional marriage plots - this feels very much like a thousand other love triangles about a thousand other characters. Ultimately this book thrives on showing us what we already know: having us exclaim - yes, it is exactly like that! Not that this is exactly a condemnation: in fact I'd probably actively go out of my way to encourage people to read The marriage plot. It is immensely readable, hugely enjoyable, exactly the right book to settle down with on a dreary afternoon, amusing, comforting, pleasurable, familiar. But just don't expect the stuff of great fiction - and Eugenides at his best - to be jolted out of your complacencies, to see the everyday rendered strange before your eyes.
