I enjoyed this book-it did remind me a lot of the Hunger Games. Tris was an interesting character and I really enjoyed the love story that was a part of this book. I am not a big fan of dysotopian literature though. It is supposed to remind us that anyday now the world can drastically change, thus altering our "normal" society. You have to think to yourself, how would I survive? Or, could I survive? Makes me want to stock up on the necessities like toilet paper and chocolate ;) The factions were interesting but extreme - I would have liked to know the background of what drastic thing forced them to create these factions-maybe that will be answered in the next book.

** spoiler alert ** So I've halfway liked these books from the start. My biggest complaint has been that all of the violence DIDN'T make you cringe. I mean, Katniss is killing children almost from the beginning, and as she does it you think, "Huh, well I guess that's another one down, good for her!" You could argue that the author did that on purpose, trying to make us feel like Katniss did, but I don't buy it. I should have felt horrified that these children were murdering each other, but I didn't. The last book fixes this, but only a little bit. Katniss starts realizing that she's been a pawn and a killing tool for various groups of people, and feels bad about it. But mostly, I think she feels bad about it because she isn't in control. I'm not a big fan of the main character. However, I really liked the ending. I was worried that the author would go for a picture-perfect happy ending or for an over-dramatic sad ending, but she did neither. I liked that Katniss lost friends (some to death, some to other circumstances) and that the love triangle was resolved in the end. I also liked that the new government wasn't the perfect solution that everyone had been hoping for. It was an altogether realistic ending to a series that I had not been taking seriously, and that was a nice surprise. But, it's still not even close to 4 stars in my book :-)
Such a bittersweet love story... Left me teary-eyed at the end
Really got a kick out of this trilogy. The audio book is a must!

A cogent if not groundbreaking look at how visual media took over the American popular imagination. Written before the internet happened, the proof of the book's basic thesis that America has become the United States of Entertainment is borne out by the fact that it applies equally well to the digital media Gabler could not have considered at the time of the book's writing.

Its very rare that I review kids books, but ever so often one comes along that my kid just loves and that we enjoy together and it's worthy of mention. The story in this is a bit dark and might not be the best for tiny kids. There's really no solid conclusion or issues being resolved like y'know...most kids books. It's very reminiscent of something written by Tim Burton or Charles Addams. The Monsterator at the end of the book is great and it's really what makes the book. My kid had a blast making different monsters and we both laughed at many of them. Lots of fun for kids!

Poison Princess locked me in a trance of mesmerizing awesome from the VERY first page. No... I'm absolutely serious. Evie has been lured into a madman's lair... And it's utterly chilling to hear his horrific and terrifying inner monologues as he tricks Evie into sliding deeper into what promises to be her worst nightmare. "My lair looks safe, warm, grandmotherly. It should; an old woman lived here before I slaughtered her and made it my home." *gasp* I know right?! The "price of entry" is that she has to recount her life before and after the Flash. He claims to be making a chronicle of events and experiences of events leading to the Flash and how people coped with the aftermath. The Flash was a catastrophic event that killed most of the world and wiped any form of vegetation right off the map. So as Evie launches into her tale, her story begins one week BEFORE the Flash and just after she was released from the mental institution. We meet the boyfriend... Who doesn't impress me too much. We meet the BFF, Melissa... "Mel was a hyperactive wild child who was a stranger to shame and had never acquainted herself with embarrassment." And we meet the band of Cajun misfits who have been thrust into suburban hell by a new bridge that put them in an entirely different school district. Jackson, the fiercest one of them all WON'T quit staring at her with his disarming grey eyes and devil may care attitude. We meet Jackson. Who. Is. EPIC. Complete with the sexiest accent I've ever READ. Seriously, usually "accents" in books tend to irritate me- but Kresley Cole did an absolutely amazing job with the authenticity, with made it even more appealing! I LOVE Evie and Javkson! There's no insta-love... No triangles... They honestly don't like each other very much! Except buried under all that hostility, is a SUPER cute romance! They trek across country, searching for Evie's grandmother and along the way they meet people from Evie's visions... Members of the Major Arcana. Evie was told long ago that she was the 'Empress' ... Then they meet 'The Moon' in the form of a super hot chick who is seemingly MADE for Jackson! Then Matthew who has made the most appearances in Evie's visions has put out a call for help, as he's DROWNING and Evie, Jack & Selena (the moon) are a state away. I KNOW. Matthew is The Fool card of the Major Arcana, and seemingly Evie's greatest friend and ally. They meet Finn, The Magican, while being held captive in a slaving camp. I loved EVERY SECOND of this book! Poison Princess is utterly mesmerizing and fiercely captivating!! Without a doubt the BEST post apocalyptic book I've read ALL YEAR!

So I will admit I watched the movie before reading the book. Now that i have read this book I sort of wished I would have read it at a younger age. It was a wonderful read. Full of adventure and great times. I think it just earned a new spot on my favorite list.

I read this one for book club so I'll save most of my comments for that. Overall, I think the book could have benefited from some subtlety. It's a dystopian parable, and I love Dave Eggers, but he kind of beats the reader over the head with the story.

Batteries Not Included by Christa Lynn is one of THE FUNNEST BOOKS I'VE READ in a VERY long time. Being single, Shelby likes to play it safe, to stay in her bubble, away from the outside world, safe. A horror novel that runs the gamut of emotions starting in the 1860s when a minister establishes a religion that eventually requires unusual sacrifices. The minister is hung by the congregation, the church sits vacant until this time when a relative purchases the building now being used as a hay storage facility and reestablishes the religion. Lots of thrills and scary moments, a new and hair raising event every chapter. A great read for the lovers of horror novels.

3.5 stars. This is not the type of book I'd usually go for but after it was shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize I thought I'd give it a shot. I really enjoyed this book. It's a very short read - I finished it in one sitting, but the story and writing style aren't overly simplistic. A haunting story that I've already spent time thinking about since I finished it - it's unsettling but in a weirdly beautiful way. I'm not sure if I wish there had been more character development or not, it may have taken away from the plot itself, but I do wish we'd got to know a bit more about the characters themselves.

Okay... Definitely different from anything I've ever read. I'm not really sure how to describe it other than weird. Never really got attached to the characters and kind of didn't care about what happened at the end. "Dear child, do you even know all the rage that is inside you?"
